subtopic_detail: Adding a specific antagonist when serotonin toxicity fails to settle with benzodiazepines and cooling
stem:
You are the emergency registrar treating a 38 year old man brought in agitated and shaking three hours after his usual evening medications. He takes sertraline for depression and was started on tramadol by a locum two days ago for back pain.

On examination he is restless and diaphoretic. His pupils are dilated, and when you dorsiflex each ankle you elicit sustained beating that is more marked in the legs than the arms. His reflexes are brisk throughout. Both offending drugs have been withheld, he has received two doses of intravenous diazepam and active surface cooling has been running for forty minutes, but his temperature and agitation have not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus greater in the lower than upper limbs, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, normal muscle bulk without rigidity of the trunk
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 620 U/L (less than 200), creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, paracetamol not detected
data_table.Treatment so far: Both serotonergic agents withheld, two doses of intravenous diazepam, active cooling for forty minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.text: Dantrolene given intravenously and repeated according to response
options.rationale: Dantrolene uncouples excitation from contraction in skeletal muscle and is used for malignant hyperthermia, where rigidity is the source of heat production. There is no evidence of benefit in serotonin toxicity and it does not address the receptor overactivity driving this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Bromocriptine given orally with continued supportive measures
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which presents with lead pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and a slower onset over days rather than the hyperreflexia and clonus seen here. Giving a dopamine agonist in serotonin toxicity may worsen it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Further escalating doses of benzodiazepine as the sole treatment
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines remain the backbone of treatment and should continue, but escalating them alone after an inadequate response leaves the serotonin receptor overactivity unopposed. Persistent hyperthermia above 38.5 degrees is the trigger to add a specific antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Oral cyproheptadine alongside active cooling and benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is a serotonin receptor antagonist and is the specific treatment when toxicity persists despite withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines and cooling. It is given enterally, by nasogastric tube if necessary, and repeated until the agitation and clonus settle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Physostigmine is the antidote for central anticholinergic toxicity, which produces dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds and urinary retention rather than the diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel sounds of serotonin toxicity. The clonus here points firmly away from an anticholinergic cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity arises when serotonergic agents are combined, and tramadol added to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is one of the commonest precipitants in Australian practice because the analgesic role of tramadol obscures its serotonergic action. The Hunter criteria diagnose it on the presence of a serotonergic agent with spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or hypertonia with hyperthermia and clonus. The lower limb predominance of clonus and hyperreflexia distinguishes it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which produces generalised lead pipe rigidity with reduced reflexes over a slower onset. Management is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care, with cyproheptadine added when hyperthermia persists and intubation with paralysis reserved for temperatures above about 39.5 degrees.
key_points: Tramadol with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor is a common Australian precipitant
Clonus and hyperreflexia predominate in the lower limbs
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome shows rigidity with reduced reflexes instead
Benzodiazepines, cooling and drug withdrawal are the first measures
Cyproheptadine is added when hyperthermia persists despite those measures
explanation.pearls: Temperature above 39.5 degrees in serotonin toxicity is an indication for intubation with neuromuscular paralysis, because muscular hyperactivity is generating the heat and antipyretics are useless against it.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent vomiting with compulsive hot bathing in a daily cannabis user after negative investigation
stem:
A 24 year old man presents to your practice after his fourth emergency department attendance this year with severe vomiting. Each episode lasts two or three days and then resolves completely, leaving him entirely well for weeks or months.

He volunteers that the only thing that settles him during an episode is standing under a shower as hot as he can bear, sometimes for an hour at a time, and that his family have complained about the water bill. He has smoked cannabis daily since he was eighteen and has cut down before without stopping. A gastroscopy, abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology arranged after his second presentation were all reported as normal, and his electrolytes between episodes are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits between episodes
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no organomegaly, well hydrated at today's review
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy, abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology all reported as normal, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Substance history: Daily cannabis use for six years, no alcohol, no other drugs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ondansetron at higher dose with admission for intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Conventional antiemetics including ondansetron characteristically perform poorly in this syndrome, and fluids treat the consequence while the cause continues. Supportive care has a place during an acute episode but is not the answer to a recurring pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Proton pump inhibitor trial with repeat gastroscopy in three months
options.rationale: Acid suppression addresses reflux or ulcer disease, and his gastroscopy has already excluded both. Repeating an investigation that was normal is unlikely to yield a different result in the absence of new features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Amitriptyline as prophylaxis for a cyclical vomiting syndrome
options.rationale: Tricyclic prophylaxis is used in idiopathic cyclical vomiting syndrome, which shares the episodic pattern but lacks the relationship to heavy cannabis use and the compulsive hot bathing behaviour. The distinction matters because removing the cannabis resolves this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Referral for gastric emptying studies before any further treatment
options.rationale: Motility studies are directed at gastroparesis, which produces persistent rather than episodic symptoms with complete well intervals, and further investigation after a normal endoscopic and imaging workup delays effective treatment. The history here is already characteristic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Advise cannabis cessation and offer topical capsaicin for episodes
options.rationale: Episodic vomiting with complete recovery between attacks, relieved specifically by compulsive hot bathing in a daily cannabis user, is diagnostic, and complete cessation is the only intervention that reliably resolves it. Topical capsaicin applied to the abdomen acts on the same receptor pathway as the hot water and provides symptomatic relief during an acute episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome is increasingly common as cannabis potency rises, and it is repeatedly misdiagnosed because the association seems counterintuitive given that cannabinoids are used therapeutically as antiemetics. The clinical signature is a cyclical pattern of severe vomiting with entirely well intervals, in a long term heavy user, with compulsive hot bathing that the patient often does not mention unless asked directly. Standard antiemetics work poorly, whereas topical capsaicin gives symptomatic relief through the same transient receptor potential vanilloid pathway that hot water stimulates, and benzodiazepines are sometimes used in the acute phase. Resolution requires complete cessation rather than reduction, and symptoms may take several weeks to settle after stopping, which should be explained in advance or the patient will conclude that cannabis was not the cause.
key_points: Episodic vomiting with well intervals in a heavy long term user is the pattern
Compulsive hot bathing is close to pathognomonic but must be asked about
Conventional antiemetics are characteristically ineffective
Topical capsaicin acts on the same receptor pathway as hot water
Only complete cessation resolves it, and symptoms may take weeks to settle
explanation.pearls: Warn patients that vomiting may continue for several weeks after stopping cannabis, because a premature return to use during that lag is the commonest reason the diagnosis is rejected by the patient.

subtopic_detail: Driving advice for an adult established on stimulant treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
stem:
A 27 year old delivery driver attends your general practice for a repeat prescription. He was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder eighteen months ago and has been on a stable dose of lisdexamfetamine prescribed by a psychiatrist for a year.

He tells you his concentration at work has improved markedly and that he has had no near misses or infringements since starting treatment. Before treatment he had two minor collisions reversing and was often described as distractible at the wheel. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiac symptoms and no other medical conditions. He has read online that he might lose his licence and is considering stopping the medication without telling his psychiatrist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable, no tremor, weight stable
data_table.Treatment: Lisdexamfetamine at a stable dose for twelve months under specialist review
data_table.Driving history: Two minor collisions before treatment, none since, no infringements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give him?

options.text: Advise him to stop driving until the stimulant has been ceased
options.rationale: Treatment improves rather than impairs driving performance in this condition, so ceasing it would raise his crash risk rather than lower it. Blanket driving restriction is not supported by the Australian fitness to drive standards for a stable treated patient. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Advise him to take a drug holiday from the stimulant on days he drives
options.rationale: Withholding the medication on driving days removes the symptom control that reduces his crash risk and is the opposite of what the evidence supports. Drug holidays are sometimes discussed for appetite or growth reasons in children, not for driving safety. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Continue the stimulant and document the fitness to drive discussion
options.rationale: Untreated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with a higher crash rate, and stimulant treatment reduces it, so a stable well controlled patient with no adverse driving history is generally fit to drive. Recording that the discussion took place, including the duty to report any condition affecting driving, is the appropriate action in general practice. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Report him to the licensing authority without discussing it with him
options.rationale: The obligation to notify rests primarily with the driver, and a doctor reporting directly is reserved for situations where the patient continues to drive against advice despite a condition that makes it unsafe. Bypassing the conversation damages the relationship without any safety gain here. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Switch him to a non stimulant agent before he drives again
options.rationale: Changing an effective and well tolerated treatment introduces a period of poorer symptom control, during which his driving risk would rise. Non stimulant agents are chosen for tolerability, misuse risk or comorbidity rather than to satisfy a driving requirement. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults is associated with a measurably higher rate of motor vehicle crashes, driven by inattention, impulsivity and risk taking, and pharmacological treatment reduces that excess risk rather than adding to it. The Australian fitness to drive standards therefore do not treat the diagnosis or its treatment as automatically disqualifying, and a stable adult on established therapy with an unremarkable driving record is generally fit for a private licence. The legal duty to report a long term condition that may affect driving sits with the licence holder, while the treating doctor advises the patient, documents that advice, and notifies the licensing authority directly only when a patient continues to drive unsafely against that advice. Commercial licence holders are assessed against a more demanding standard, and stimulant misuse or diversion, substance use disorder and untreated symptoms are the features that actually raise concern.
key_points: Untreated symptoms raise crash risk while effective treatment lowers it
Neither the diagnosis nor stimulant treatment is automatically disqualifying
The duty to notify the licensing authority rests with the driver
Direct medical notification is reserved for continued unsafe driving against advice
Commercial licence holders are assessed against a stricter standard
explanation.pearls: Document the specific advice given about driving and the patient's obligation to notify, because that contemporaneous note is what protects the clinician if a crash later occurs.

subtopic_detail: Feature that separates schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29 year old man in the community clinic. Over three years he has had two admissions with elevated mood, reduced sleep and grandiose beliefs that he had been chosen to reform the banking system, and one prolonged period of low mood.

His case manager has kept a daily mood chart. It shows that over the past eight months he has had two stretches of six to eight weeks in which his mood ratings, sleep and activity were all within his normal range. His mother reports that during those same stretches he continued to hear two voices commenting on his actions and remained convinced that his neighbours were reporting on him to a government agency. His urine drug screens have been negative throughout and his thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Mood chart: Two periods of six to eight weeks with mood, sleep and activity ratings within his normal range
data_table.Mental state during euthymic periods: Persistent second person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screens negative on repeated testing, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.History: Two manic admissions and one depressive episode over three years

lead_in: Which feature best supports a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features?

options.text: Grandiose delusions occurring during his periods of elevated mood
options.rationale: Mood congruent delusions during a manic episode are entirely typical of bipolar disorder with psychotic features and do not distinguish between the two diagnoses. Their presence is expected in both. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Delusions and hallucinations persisting while his mood was euthymic
options.rationale: The defining requirement is psychotic symptoms lasting two weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode, while mood symptoms are present for the majority of the illness overall. His documented six to eight week euthymic stretches with continuing hallucinations and delusions satisfy exactly this criterion. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: A family history of bipolar disorder in his mother and maternal uncle
options.rationale: Family history informs risk but does not determine which diagnosis applies to an individual, and the genetic contributions to schizoaffective and bipolar disorder overlap substantially. It cannot settle the distinction. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Poor response of his psychotic symptoms to lithium used on its own
options.rationale: Treatment response is not a diagnostic criterion, and incomplete response to monotherapy occurs across both conditions. Reasoning backwards from a drug response is a recognised source of diagnostic error. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Onset of his first psychotic episode in his early twenties at university
options.rationale: Early adult onset is the typical age of presentation for both conditions and for schizophrenia, so it carries no discriminating value. Age alone never separates these diagnoses. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: The boundary between schizoaffective disorder and a mood disorder with psychotic features is drawn by the temporal relationship between psychosis and mood, not by the content or severity of either. In bipolar disorder with psychotic features the psychotic symptoms occur only within mood episodes and remit as the mood normalises, whereas schizoaffective disorder requires a period of at least two weeks in which delusions or hallucinations persist without a major mood episode. A second requirement prevents the diagnosis drifting towards schizophrenia: mood episodes must be present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. Making the distinction properly requires longitudinal information, which is why mood charts and collateral history carry more weight than any single cross sectional assessment, and it matters because it shapes long term prognosis and the balance between mood stabilising and antipsychotic treatment.
key_points: Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features
Schizoaffective disorder requires two weeks of psychosis without a major mood episode
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total illness duration
Longitudinal data and collateral history are needed for the distinction
Substance use and thyroid disease must be excluded before the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A mood chart maintained over months is the single most useful diagnostic instrument here, because the diagnosis turns on whether psychosis and mood disturbance overlap in time rather than on any feature visible at a single interview.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders
